description: Hospital pharmacy operations: cold chain, controlled substances, recalls, returns and sterile compounding.

units.title: Cold-chain storage
units.text: Refrigerated medicines are stored between 2 °C and 8 °C. Each refrigerator has a continuous data logger that records the temperature every five minutes and raises an alarm at the pharmacy desk when a reading leaves the range.

units.title: Temperature excursions
units.text: If a refrigerator stays above 8 °C for more than 30 minutes, the affected stock is quarantined rather than discarded. The pharmacist on duty contacts the manufacturer, and the stock is released only after written confirmation that it remains stable.

units.title: Frozen vaccines are not reused
units.text: Freezing destroys the potency of most vaccines even when the vial looks normal after thawing. A vaccine that has frozen is destroyed and recorded as pharmaceutical waste; it never goes back into stock.

units.title: Dispensing Schedule II substances
units.text: Two licensed staff members take part in every Schedule II dispensing: one prepares the medicine and the other checks the quantity and the patient before handover. The second person signs the electronic register before the end of the same shift.

units.title: Shift-change vault count
units.text: At every shift change the outgoing and the incoming pharmacist count the vault together and both sign the count sheet. A discrepancy is reported to the pharmacy director within one hour, and the vault stays locked until the count is reconciled.

units.title: Par level
units.text: The minimum quantity of a medicine that a ward keeps on hand to cover expected use until the next scheduled delivery. When the counted stock falls below this quantity, the inventory system creates a replenishment request automatically.

units.title: Look-alike, sound-alike (LASA) medicines
units.text: Medicines whose names or packaging are easily confused with another product. They are kept on separate shelves, never next to each other, and their labels use tall-man lettering such as hydrOXYzine and hydrALAZINE.

units.title: Tall-man lettering
units.text: Capitalising the letters that differ draws attention to the part of the name that distinguishes two drugs. This reduces selection errors at the shelf and on the dispensing screen.

units.title: Recall response matrix
units.text:
| Recall class | Action | Deadline |
|---|---|---|
| Class I | Remove every unit and notify the prescribers | Within 4 hours |
| Class II | Remove the affected lots | Within 24 hours |
| Class III | Remove during the next scheduled shelf check | Within 7 days |

units.title: Medicines returned by patients
units.text: Medicines returned by patients are never dispensed again, even when the package is sealed, because the pharmacy cannot verify how they were stored outside the hospital. They are sent to pharmaceutical waste.

units.title: Short-dated stock
units.text: Stock that expires within 90 days is moved to the front of the shelf and flagged in the inventory system. Expired stock is removed on the first working day of each month.

units.title: Monthly pharmacy indicators
units.text:
| Indicator | Target | Last month |
|---|---|---|
| Dispensing errors per 10,000 items | Below 2 | 1.4 |
| Cold-chain excursions | 0 | 3 |
| Vault count discrepancies | 0 | 1 |

units.title: Sterile compounding requires a certified hood
headingPath: Sterile compounding requires a certified hood
units.text: Intravenous admixtures are prepared inside an ISO Class 5 laminar airflow hood. The hood is recertified every six months, and a failed certification suspends sterile compounding until the hood is repaired and passes again.

units.title: Night shift coverage
units.text: From 22:00 to 07:00 a single pharmacist covers the whole hospital. Urgent orders are handled first; routine ward restocking waits for the morning team.
